defs_parts: Six labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow.
In the glossary: the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it.
Video only: the term comes from a video lecture, and is not in the course text or on the term list.
Computed: the numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs.
Simulation: a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game.
Illustrative data: numbers chosen to show the idea, not measured.
Conceptual: a drawing of the idea, with no data behind it.
recap_lines: A game rests on three pillars, the player, communication and appeal.
Communication shows the goal, and guiding the focus shows where to look now.
Linear has one route, and nonlinear lets the player choose between routes.
Anticipation is a short warning, and build-up is a long rise in tension.
Consistent rules bend physics the same way every time.
Progression is the overall rise, and pacing swings between calm and intense.
bookends.command: Quiz me on game design terms with short cases from making a platformer, one at a time. Use the terms communication, guiding the focus, linear, nonlinear, side quest, anticipation, build-up, consistent rules, progression and pacing. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me if I was right.
checks: Check: each case is a game-making situation, and the answer waits for you.
Check: you named the exact term and said why its look-alike is wrong.

The exact term turns a vague complaint about a level into an instruction you can act on.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Newcomers often say that good pacing means the challenge keeps rising. That rise is progression. Pacing is the swing between intense and calm moments, a hard fight and then a rest. A straight climb wears the player out. This film goes through the terms of guidance, fairness and rhythm, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.

beats.narration_text: This drawing is a building on three columns, and the first column, Player, has risen in red. The Three pillars are what a game rests on, the player's role, communication and appeal. The first is Player purpose, what the player does and why. The player, not the game, pushes things forward. For example, in a platformer like Walker the purpose is to reach the goal flag, and every jump is the player's own choice.

beats.narration_text: The second pillar, Communication, now stands. Without it the player does not know the goal or how to reach it, and feels powerless. The box at the bottom sets it against player purpose. Purpose is what you do and why, and communication is showing you what and how. For example, a goal flag that waves at the far end of the first screen, with a row of coins arching over the first gap, shows a new player both.

beats.narration_text: The third pillar, Appeal, rises in red, and the roof, the game itself, rests on all three. Appeal is the pull to keep playing. It is the hardest of the three to guarantee, and the most important. For example, if your playtesters finish the first level and ask to play it again, it has appeal. If they put the controller down halfway, it may not.

beats.narration_text: Now the door is lit in red, with a ring of light around it. Guiding the focus means making clear what the player should concentrate on right now. beats.narration_text: A chain of rooms, from start to end. Linear and nonlinear describe the route through a level. Linear means one route from start to end, each room opening onto the next. Here there is exactly one route. A linear level is easy to guide, and the designer controls the pace. For example, a tutorial level where the player can only run right, from the first platform to the goal flag, is linear.

beats.narration_text: Now the chain has two forks. Nonlinear means the player chooses between routes. Each fork offers two ways through, so two times two gives four routes from start to end. For example, a level where the player picks a high path over the rooftops or a low path through the sewer, and later picks again between a ladder and a lift, is nonlinear.

beats.narration_text: Back to one main line, with one red room off to the side. A Side quest is a detour from the main storyline. It leaves the main line and returns to the same place, so the main story still holds. That gives two ways to finish, with the detour or without it. For example, a cave off the main path, where the player can rescue a lost miner for a reward and then return to the road, is a side quest.

beats.narration_text: A red staircase climbs as the player learns skills along a famous first level, World one-one. Level design is planning and building the spaces the player moves through. Teaching through levels means the first level lets the player try each skill, with no text. Here seven skills are taught with no tutorial words. For example, level design places the floor, spikes and goal flag of a Walker level, and a level can teach by setting a small, harmless gap before the first deadly one.

beats.narration_text: Two timelines of an enemy attack, one with no warning and one with a grey wind-up before the red hit. Anticipation means preparing the player for what comes next. In this made-up example, with an assumed reaction time of a quarter of a second, a half-second wind-up leaves a quarter of a second to spare. No wind-up leaves none, and the hit feels cheap. For example, an enemy that crouches and flashes before it lunges gives the player anticipation.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap. A game rests on three pillars, the player, communication and appeal. Communication shows the goal, and guiding the focus shows where to look now. Linear has one route, and nonlinear lets the player choose between routes. Anticipation is a short warning, and build-up is a long rise in tension. Consistent rules bend physics the same way every time. Progression is the overall rise, and pacing swings between calm and intense.
